walkthroughs.body_html: The Communist Party Historians' Group (1946-56) including Christopher Hill, Eric Hobsbawm, Rodney Hilton and E.P. Thompson reframed English history through class. Hill's The World Turned Upside Down (1972) recovered radical sects of the Civil War. Hobsbawm's Age of trilogy (1962-87) provided a sweeping account of capitalist modernity. Thompson's Making of the English Working Class (1963) rejected determinism, emphasising worker self-formation.

Marc Bloch (Feudal Society, 1939-40) and Lucien Febvre founded Annales in 1929, rejecting narrow political narrative. Fernand Braudel's Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) introduced three temporal layers: environmental longue duree, conjunctural and event-level. Third-generation Annalistes like Le Roy Ladurie (Montaillou, 1975) explored peasant mentalities, anticipating cultural history.

From the 1970s, social history fragmented into women's history (Sheila Rowbotham), Black history, microhistory and the linguistic turn. Joan Scott's 1986 article 'Gender' demanded analysis of power in discourse. Critics such as Lawrence Stone in 1979 detected a 'revival of narrative'. The field's pluralism reflects post-1968 challenges to grand narrative, even as quantitative cliometrics persisted in economic history.
